title: Algebra, Trigonometry & Precalculus Toolkit
subject: Algebra & Precalc
summary: A fast, targeted rebuild of the algebra, function, trig and estimation skills that calculus and physics assume, aimed at a chemist who has the ideas but has lost the reflexes. Ends with the dimensional-analysis and small-quantity approximation habits physicists use daily.

units.title: Algebraic Fluency
units.summary: Rebuild the manipulation reflexes physics assumes: exponent and radical rules, factoring, completing the square, linear systems, inequalities and absolute values; chemists use these daily in equilibrium and kinetics algebra.

lessons.title: Exponent laws, fractional exponents, and radicals
objectives: Simplify expressions using the exponent laws (product, quotient, power, negative and zero exponents) without a calculator, including fractional exponents such as x^(3/2).
Convert fluently between radical form and rational-exponent form and rationalise a denominator.

lectures.title: More rational exponents and exponent laws

demoIdeas: Sliders for base a and exponents m, n: bars show a^m, a^n and a^(m+n) on a log-scaled axis, with fractional exponents drawn as roots (x^(3/2) as the square root cubed).

lessons.title: Rational expressions, rearranging formulas, and avoiding standard algebra errors
objectives: Add, subtract, multiply and divide rational expressions by finding a common denominator and cancelling only common factors.
Rearrange a formula to isolate a chosen variable (e.g. solve PV = nRT for T, or K = [C][D]/([A][B]) for [D]) and state each algebraic step's justification.
Identify and avoid the standard algebra errors: (a+b)^2 = a^2+b^2, cancelling terms instead of factors, and dropping the square-root sign ambiguity.

lessons.title: Factoring, completing the square, and quadratics in disguise
objectives: Factor polynomials using greatest common factor, difference of squares/cubes, and trinomial methods.
Complete the square for ax^2+bx+c and read off the vertex and the axis of symmetry.
Solve equations that are quadratic in disguise by substitution (e.g. x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0).

lectures.title: Worked example: Rewriting expressions by completing the square
Worked example: Solving equations by completing the square
Introduction to factoring higher degree polynomials

demoIdeas: Quadratic playground: sliders for a, b, c redraw the parabola and show the completed-square form, vertex and factored form, with the roots appearing or merging as the parameters change.

lessons.title: The quadratic formula, the discriminant, and equilibrium quadratics
objectives: Derive the quadratic formula by completing the square and use the discriminant to predict the number and type of roots.
Solve a quadratic equilibrium expression (e.g. x^2/(c-x) = K for a weak acid) and decide which root is physically admissible.

lectures.title: How to use the quadratic formula

demoIdeas: Sliders for K and the initial concentration c in x^2/(c - x) = K: plot the parabola x^2 + Kx - Kc, mark both roots, highlight the physically admissible one in [0, c], and show the sign of the discriminant.

lessons.title: Linear systems by substitution and elimination, and mixing problems
objectives: Solve systems of two and three linear equations by substitution and elimination and recognise inconsistent and dependent systems.
Set up and solve a mixing, stoichiometry or dilution word problem as a linear system (e.g. two solutions combined to a target concentration).

readings.title: Systems of Linear Equations: Two Variables
Systems of Linear Equations: Three Variables

lectures.title: Systems of equations word problems example 1

demoIdeas: Drag the coefficients of two lines ax + by = c and watch the intersection move, turn into parallel lines (no solution) or collapse into one line (infinitely many); a second panel mixes two stock solutions with a volume slider against the target concentration.

lessons.title: Inequalities, intervals, absolute values, and sign analysis
objectives: Solve linear and compound inequalities, expressing the answer as an interval, and explain when the inequality sign flips.
Solve equations and inequalities involving |x - a| by splitting into cases or using the distance interpretation.
Solve a quadratic or rational inequality by sign analysis on intervals.

lectures.title: Solving rational inequalities by testing intervals rational expression on both sides

demoIdeas: Number-line inequality solver: type an inequality and see the solution set shaded with open/closed endpoints; |x - a| < delta is drawn as an interval of radius delta, with a sign chart for rational inequalities.

units.title: Functions and Graphs
units.summary: Function notation, domain and range, composition, inverses, transformations of graphs, polynomials and rational functions; the vocabulary every later calculus and physics derivation is written in.

lessons.title: Function notation, domain and range, and functions as physical relations
objectives: Evaluate a function given by formula, table or graph, and use the vertical line test to decide whether a relation is a function.
Determine the domain and range of a function built from polynomials, radicals, quotients and logarithms.
Distinguish a function from its value, and write a physical relation (e.g. P(V) at fixed T) as a function with stated domain.

lectures.title: Domain and range of a function given a formula
Domain and range of a function

demoIdeas: Type f(x) and see its graph with the domain shaded on the x-axis and the range on the y-axis; a vertical line sweeps across and turns red where the relation fails the vertical line test.

lessons.title: Composition and inverse functions
objectives: Form f(g(x)) and g(f(x)), determine the domain of a composite, and decompose a composite into inner and outer functions (the skill behind the chain rule).
Decide whether a function is one-to-one, find its inverse algebraically, and sketch the inverse as a reflection across y = x.
demoIdeas: Composition machine: pick f and g, drag an input along the axis and see f(g(x)) traced through both boxes, plus a toggle that reflects the graph across y = x to show the inverse and where it fails one-to-one.

lessons.title: Graph transformations, even and odd symmetry, and piecewise functions
objectives: Sketch y = a f(b(x - h)) + k from the graph of f by applying shifts, stretches and reflections in the correct order.
Classify a function as even, odd, or neither algebraically and from its graph, and state what that implies for the integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval (to be proved later).
Write a piecewise function (e.g. the potential of a step barrier) and graph it, marking open and closed endpoints.

lectures.title: How to evaluate a piecewise function (example)

demoIdeas: Transformation sandbox: sliders for a, b, h, k applied to a library of parent functions, with even/odd symmetry detected live and a piecewise barrier potential editor with open/closed endpoints.

lessons.title: Average rate of change, secant slopes, and increasing or decreasing behaviour
objectives: Compute the average rate of change (slope of a secant line) of a function over an interval and interpret its units.
Identify intervals of increase/decrease and local extrema from a graph and relate them to the sign of the rate of change.

readings.title: Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs

lectures.title: Introduction to average rate of change
Finding average rate of change of polynomials
How to find the average rate of change from a table

demoIdeas: Drag two points on a curve: the secant line and its slope (with units) update, and the secant turns into the tangent as the points merge; shade increasing and decreasing intervals.

lessons.title: Polynomial division, rational zeros, and the fundamental theorem of algebra
objectives: Divide polynomials using long division and synthetic division and state the remainder theorem and factor theorem.
Find all rational zeros of a polynomial with the rational zeros theorem, and use multiplicity to describe end behaviour and the graph at each zero.
Explain why the fundamental theorem of algebra implies that an nth-degree polynomial has n complex roots counted with multiplicity.
demoIdeas: Edit zeros and multiplicities of a polynomial and watch the graph cross or touch the axis at each; a draggable test point a shows p(a) equal to the remainder of division by (x - a).

lessons.title: Rational functions: asymptotes, holes, and partial fractions
objectives: Find vertical, horizontal and oblique asymptotes and holes of a rational function and sketch its graph.
Decompose a proper rational function into partial fractions (distinct linear, repeated linear, and irreducible quadratic factors), the algebra used later in integration and Laplace transforms.

lectures.title: Partial Fractions I (cover-up method for distinct linear factors)
Partial Fractions I (repeated and quadratic factors)

demoIdeas: Rational-function explorer: edit numerator and denominator roots and see vertical asymptotes, holes and end behaviour update live, with the partial-fraction terms plotted separately and summing to the original.

units.title: Exponentials and Logarithms
units.summary: Exponential and logarithmic functions, their laws, and modelling with them; the language of Arrhenius kinetics, Beer-Lambert absorbance, pH, half-lives and Boltzmann factors.

lessons.title: Exponentials, logarithms, the log laws, and the number e
objectives: Graph y = b^x and y = log_b x, state their domains and ranges, and explain why they are inverses.
Apply the three log laws (product, quotient, power) and the change-of-base formula to expand, combine, and evaluate logarithms by hand.
Define e as the base for which d/dx of b^x equals b^x (previewing calculus) and convert any base to base e via b^x = e^(x ln b).

lectures.title: What's so special about Euler's number e?

demoIdeas: Log-scale slider: move a point on a number line and watch x, log10 x and ln x update together; sliders for the base b show b^x and log_b x as mirror images across y = x, with pH as -log10[H+].

lessons.title: Solving exponential and log equations: pH and Arrhenius
objectives: Solve exponential and logarithmic equations, and check for extraneous solutions.
Use logs for chemistry: compute pH from [H+], and solve the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT) for Ea given two rate constants at two temperatures.

lectures.title: pH, pOH of strong acids and bases

demoIdeas: Slider for [H+] on a log axis reads off pH; an Arrhenius panel lets you drag two (T, k) points and shows ln k against 1/T with the slope giving E_a.

lessons.title: Exponential growth and decay: half-life, Beer-Lambert, and continuous compounding
objectives: Model growth or decay as N(t) = N0 e^(kt) and convert between the rate constant k, the half-life, and the doubling time.
Apply Beer-Lambert A = epsilon l c and radioactive decay as the same exponential-decay mathematics.
Solve compound-interest and continuous-compounding problems and recognise that (1 + 1/n)^n tends to e.

lectures.title: Introduction to compound interest and e

demoIdeas: Sliders for k and N0: N(t) is plotted with its half-life marked, and a toggle redraws it on a log axis as a straight line; a Beer-Lambert tab shows absorbance against concentration and transmitted fraction.

lessons.title: Semi-log and log-log plots: linearising kinetics and Arrhenius data
objectives: Use semi-log and log-log plots to turn exponentials and power laws into straight lines and extract the parameters from the slope and intercept.
Linearise first-order kinetics data (ln[A] versus t) and an Arrhenius data set (ln k versus 1/T) and extract k and Ea from a fit.
demoIdeas: Fit-a-line lab: generate noisy exponential and power-law data and toggle linear, semi-log and log-log axes to see which one straightens it, reading k or the exponent from the fitted slope.

units.title: Trigonometry
units.summary: Angles and radians, the unit circle, the six trig functions and their inverses, graphs of sinusoids, identities, and solving triangles: the geometry behind waves, orbitals, and rotations.

lessons.title: Radians, arc length, sector area, and angular velocity
objectives: Convert between degrees and radians and compute arc length s = r theta and sector area A = r^2 theta / 2.
Compute angular velocity omega = theta / t and relate it to linear speed v = r omega.

lectures.title: Finding arc length from radian angle measure

demoIdeas: Drag a point around a circle: the angle in degrees and radians, arc length r*theta and sector area update, and a velocity arrow of length r*omega appears for a chosen angular speed.

lessons.title: The unit circle: special angles, reference angles, and the Pythagorean identity
objectives: State from memory the sine and cosine of 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees (and equivalents in radians) and extend them to all four quadrants using reference angles.
Define cos theta and sin theta as the coordinates of a point on the unit circle and derive the identity sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.
Identify the quadrant of an angle and the sign of each trig function there.

readings.title: Unit Circle: Sine and Cosine Functions

lectures.title: Finding trig functions of special angles example
Pythagorean trig identity from unit circle

demoIdeas: Unit-circle explorer: drag the angle around the circle and see the (cos, sin) point, the signs by quadrant, the reference angle and the sine and cosine graphs unrolling.

lessons.title: Right-triangle trigonometry and the six trig functions
objectives: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find unknown sides and angles of a right triangle and resolve a vector into components.
Define tan, cot, sec, csc from sin and cos and state their domains and signs by quadrant.
demoIdeas: Triangle-in-circle: a right triangle whose hypotenuse sweeps the unit circle, with all six functions drawn as labelled line segments and a vector resolved into components.

lessons.title: Inverse trig functions, principal values, and restricted domains
objectives: Define arcsin, arccos, arctan, state their principal-value ranges, and evaluate expressions such as sin(arccos x) by drawing a triangle.
Explain why a restricted domain is needed for an inverse trig function, using the horizontal line test.

lectures.title: Restricting domain of trig function to make invertible

demoIdeas: Plot sin x with a draggable restriction interval and its reflection across y = x: only the principal interval passes the horizontal line test, and arcsin(sin x) is traced as x sweeps beyond it.

lessons.title: Graphing sinusoids and the other trig functions: amplitude, period, phase
objectives: Read amplitude, period, angular frequency, phase shift and midline from y = A sin(Bx - C) + D and sketch it.
Write a sinusoid from a graph or from a verbal description (e.g. a mass on a spring at t = 0 at maximum displacement).
Graph tan, cot, sec, csc, identifying the vertical asymptotes and period of each.

readings.title: Graphs of the Sine and Cosine Functions
Graphs of the Other Trigonometric Functions

lectures.title: Midline, amplitude and period of a function
Example: Amplitude and period cosine transformations

demoIdeas: Sliders for A, B, h and D on sine, cosine and tangent: the graph updates with the amplitude, period, phase shift, midline and asymptotes annotated.

lessons.title: Frequency, angular frequency, and simple harmonic motion x(t)
objectives: Relate frequency f, angular frequency omega, and period T by omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi / T and give the units of each.
Model simple harmonic motion x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi) and explain the physical meaning of phi.
demoIdeas: Wave dial: sliders for amplitude, frequency and phase of x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi), with a spring-mass animation moving by the same x(t) and a second oscillator with its own phase beside it.

lessons.title: Proving identities, the sum and difference formulas, and double angles
objectives: Prove the Pythagorean, reciprocal and quotient identities and derive 1 + tan^2 = sec^2 from sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.
Verify an identity by transforming one side only, without assuming the result.
Use the sum and difference formulas for sine and cosine, and derive the double-angle and half-angle formulas from them.

lectures.title: Proof of angle addition formula for cosine
Proof of angle addition formula for sine
Applying angle addition formula for sin
Pythagorean trig identity from soh cah toa

demoIdeas: Two draggable angles a and b on the unit circle build cos(a + b) and sin(a + b) geometrically, with a live numeric check of the sum and double-angle formulas.

lessons.title: Power reduction, product-to-sum, and beats
objectives: Rewrite sin^2 and cos^2 in terms of cos 2theta (the power-reduction formulas), the move that makes integrals like the integral of sin^2 doable.
Convert products to sums and sums to products, e.g. to see beats between two close frequencies.

lectures.title: Double angle formula for cosine example

demoIdeas: Beats demo: add two cosines of nearby frequencies and show the sum, the product-form envelope 2cos((a - b)t/2), the audible beat, and the average of sin^2 settling at 1/2.

lessons.title: Trig equations, the laws of sines and cosines, and triangle area
objectives: Solve trigonometric equations, finding all solutions in an interval and the general solution with +2 pi n.
Use the law of sines and law of cosines to solve a non-right triangle, and the ambiguous case of SSA.
Compute the area of a triangle as (1/2) a b sin C.
demoIdeas: Drag triangle vertices to see law of sines and cosines values update, with an SSA mode where a side swings to show 0, 1 or 2 triangles; a second panel intersects y = sin x with a horizontal line to show all solutions.

lessons.title: The small-angle approximation and the pendulum
objectives: State and justify, numerically, the small-angle approximations sin theta ~ theta, tan theta ~ theta, cos theta ~ 1 - theta^2/2, and give the error at 5 and 20 degrees.
Apply the small-angle approximation to the pendulum to turn the nonlinear equation into simple harmonic motion.
demoIdeas: Pendulum simulation with an amplitude slider overlaying the exact motion and the SHM prediction so the period drift appears at large angle; a gauge plots sin theta against theta with the percentage error.

units.title: Complex Numbers, Vectors, and Coordinates
units.summary: Complex arithmetic and polar form (the gateway to Euler's formula and wavefunctions), vectors, and polar and parametric coordinates.

lessons.title: Complex arithmetic, conjugates, and polar form
objectives: Add, multiply, divide and conjugate complex numbers z = a + bi and compute |z|, arg z, and Re and Im parts.
Convert between rectangular and polar form z = r e^(i theta) and multiply and divide in polar form by multiplying moduli and adding angles.

lectures.title: Rectangular to polar form of complex number
Dividing complex numbers in polar form

demoIdeas: Argand diagram: drag z and w to see z + w by the parallelogram, z*w by adding angles and multiplying lengths, and the conjugate as a reflection across the real axis.

lessons.title: Euler's formula, De Moivre's theorem, and complex roots
objectives: State Euler's formula e^(i theta) = cos theta + i sin theta, and use it to re-derive the sum formulas for sine and cosine.
Find all n roots of z^n = w using De Moivre's theorem and place them on the complex plane.
Explain why a complex quadratic has conjugate roots when the coefficients are real and how this relates to oscillating solutions (chemistry: the phase factors in wavefunctions like e^(ikx)).
demoIdeas: Sliders for n and w: the n roots of z^n = w appear as vertices of a regular polygon; e^(i theta) animates around the unit circle with its cosine and sine projections.

lessons.title: Vectors, components, and the dot product
objectives: Represent a vector in components and in magnitude-direction form and add, subtract and scale vectors geometrically and algebraically.
Compute dot products and use them to find the angle between two vectors and the component of one along another.

lectures.title: Vector dot product and vector length

demoIdeas: Drag two arrows in the plane: the dot product, angle, projection of one on the other and the work F.d update live.

lessons.title: Polar coordinates and parametric curves
objectives: Convert between polar (r, theta) and rectangular (x, y) coordinates and sketch simple polar curves (circle, cardioid, rose).
Describe a curve parametrically (x(t), y(t)) and eliminate the parameter, e.g. for projectile motion and circular motion.
demoIdeas: Polar grapher and conic sliders: type r(theta) and trace the curve with the matching (x, y) point, then sliders for a, b in x = a cos t, y = b sin t and the eccentricity show ellipse, parabola and hyperbola morphing into one another.

lessons.title: Conic sections: ellipse, parabola and hyperbola
objectives: Write the equation of a conic in rectangular form and recognise ellipse, parabola and hyperbola from the equation (orbits, preview).
Read the centre, semi-axes and foci of an ellipse from x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 and relate a, b, c and the eccentricity e = c/a.

units.title: Estimation, Dimensions, and Approximation
units.summary: Dimensional analysis, order-of-magnitude estimation, sequences and the binomial theorem, and small-quantity approximations: the habits that let physicists check and simplify a result before computing it.

lessons.title: Dimensions and dimensional analysis: consistency checks and scaling laws
objectives: Express a physical quantity's dimensions in M, L, T (and temperature, charge) and check that every equation is dimensionally consistent.
Use dimensional analysis to derive the scaling of a result, e.g. the period of a pendulum T ~ sqrt(l/g), or the radius of a blast wave from energy and density, up to a dimensionless constant.
demoIdeas: Dimension checker: type an equation with unit-tagged symbols and see the dimension of each term, flagging mismatches; a pendulum slider for length and mass shows only length changes the period.

lessons.title: Unit conversion, Fermi estimates, and dimensionless groups
objectives: Convert units reliably, including between SI and cgs and between J/mol, eV and kcal/mol.
Make a Fermi estimate (e.g. number of molecules in a breath, or atoms in a grain of salt) by decomposing it into factors, stating uncertainty in orders of magnitude.
Use a dimensionless group (such as E/kT, the Boltzmann factor argument) to decide which regime a problem is in.
demoIdeas: Fermi chain builder: drag factors into a product and watch the order-of-magnitude result with its propagated log-uncertainty; an E/kT slider shows the Boltzmann populations of two levels switching regime.

lessons.title: Sequences, series and the geometric sum
objectives: Evaluate sigma notation and sum an arithmetic series.
Sum a finite geometric series and the infinite geometric series with |r| < 1.

lectures.title: Sum of an infinite geometric series
Worked example: finite geometric series (sigma notation)

demoIdeas: Slider for the ratio r: partial sums of a geometric series converge or run away, with the 1/(1 - r) limit marked; Pascal's triangle highlights C(n, k) and a bar chart shows the arrangements of k excited sites among n.

lessons.title: The binomial theorem and counting arrangements
objectives: Expand (a + b)^n with the binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle, and compute binomial coefficients nCk.
Count arrangements and combinations with factorials (preview of statistical mechanics counting of microstates).

lectures.title: Connecting Pascal's triangle to binomial combinatorics

lessons.title: The binomial approximation for small quantities and its error
objectives: Use the binomial approximation (1 + x)^p ~ 1 + p x for |x| << 1 to simplify expressions such as 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) and gravitational potential corrections.
Estimate the error of a first- or second-order approximation by comparing against the exact value on a calculator.

lectures.title: Introduction to Linear Approximation (the (1+x)^r approximation and worked examples)

demoIdeas: Binomial approximation scope: plot (1 + x)^p and the 1 + px line; sliders for x and p show the percentage error as x grows.
